geneSetsToRegionSets

Source: R/geneSets.R
geneSetsToRegionSets.Rd

Turns gene sets into region sets, by mapping every gene of a set through the links stored by annotateRegions, so that a pathway becomes the regions assigned to its genes and can be handed straight to testRegionSets.

This is what makes pathway-level testing of differential regions go through camera and fry rather than through a ranked gene list. The directionality problem that ordinarily has to be solved before a gene list can be written, one gene carrying several regions moving in different directions, is not solved here: it is left to the test, which reports a self-contained and a mixed p-value and so answers it rather than deciding it in advance.

Usage

geneSetsToRegionSets(
  object,
  geneSets,
  minWeight = NULL,
  linkType = NULL,
  minRegions = 2,
  maxRegions = NULL,
  regionSets = NULL,
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

object

RegionSetDE.counts, RegionSetDE.fit or RegionSetDE.results object carrying the links.

geneSets

Named list of gene identifiers, one element per set, or a two-column table naming the set and the gene.

minWeight

Numeric value with the smallest link.weight a link must carry to be used. Default: NULL, every link is used whatever its weight.

linkType

Character vector with the kinds of link to follow, among "promoter" and "distal" as annotateRegions labelled them with its tssRegion. This is how the promoter-proximal and the distal analysis are run separately. Default: NULL, every link.

minRegions

Numeric value with the smallest number of regions a set must reach to be returned. Note that this counts regions and not genes. Default: 2, the fewest a set level test can work with.

maxRegions

Numeric value with the largest number of regions a set may reach. Default: NULL, no upper bound.

regionSets

Character vector with the names of the region sets the regions are taken from, which is how the analysis is restricted to one class of element, promoters for instance. Default: NULL, every set of the object.

verbose

Logical value to indicate whether the messages must be printed. Default: TRUE.

Value

A named list of character vectors, one element per gene set, holding the keys of the regions reached by that set. The keys are the set name and the region identifier pasted with a vertical bar, which is the form testRegionSets accepts through its regionSets argument. A geneSetSummary attribute carries one row per set with the number of genes it holds, the number of them the links reach, and the number of regions.

Details

Gene sets overlap and region sets of this package do not. A promoter belonging to fifty pathways is one row of the object that fifty sets reach, which is why this returns keys rather than a GRangesList: a list of ranges would have to repeat the row fifty times, and the counting would then be wrong in fifty ways. testRegionSets resolves the keys against its own rows, after any collapsing of the tiles, so the sets stay correct whatever the counting level.

The comparison universe follows from that. With sets supplied this way, each one is compared against every other row of the object rather than against the other sets, which is the right comparison for a pathway: the question is whether the regions of this pathway moved more than the regions of the rest of the genome that was tested, not whether they moved more than the regions of the other pathways. It also means the universe is the annotated and tested regions and nothing wider, which is the background any enrichment of this kind should have and the one most often got wrong.

What this does not fix is the bias that comes before it. A gene with a long regulatory locus carries more regions than a gene with a short one, so a set rich in such genes reaches more rows, and camera corrects for the correlation between those rows without correcting for how many of them there are. Where that matters, compare the result against a count-based method built for it, chipenrich or polyenrich for instance, run on the regions rather than on the genes.

minWeight is the one place a link weight is used, and it is used as a filter rather than as a weight: neither camera nor fry accepts a per-region weight, so a contact probability can decide whether a link is trusted enough to be followed and cannot make one link count more than another. Asking for it on links that carry no weight stops, rather than silently keeping everything, since a filter that quietly does nothing is worse than one that is not there.

Splitting promoter-proximal from distal links is usually worth doing, and there are two ways to reach it. linkType filters the links themselves, on the labels annotateRegions wrote from its tssRegion, which is the route when the regions are one undifferentiated set of peaks. regionSets selects whole region sets instead, which is the route when they were already split at load time, by loadConsensusPeaks(regionSets = , regionMode = "split") for instance. Either way the point is the same: promoter-proximal and distal regions of one gene behave differently often enough that mixing them is where much of the apparent disagreement within a gene comes from.

See also

annotateRegions, regionLinks, testRegionSets

Author

Sebastian Gregoricchio

Examples

counts <- loadExampleData("counts", verbose = FALSE)

regionTable <- as.data.frame(SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(counts))[1:8, 1:3]
linkTable <- data.frame(regionTable,
                        gene.id = c("geneA", "geneA", "geneB", "geneB",
                                    "geneC", "geneC", "geneD", "geneD"))

counts <- annotateRegions(counts, linkTable = linkTable, verbose = FALSE)

geneSets <- list(pathwayOne = c("geneA", "geneB"),
                 pathwayTwo = c("geneC", "geneD", "geneE"))

regionSets <- geneSetsToRegionSets(counts, geneSets = geneSets, verbose = FALSE)
lengths(regionSets)
#> pathwayOne pathwayTwo 
#>          4          4 
attr(regionSets, "geneSetSummary")
#>     set.name n.genes n.genes.linked n.regions
#> 1 pathwayOne       2              2         4
#> 2 pathwayTwo       3              2         4
